passage: Zeynep's teacher in Istanbul said the class could not go to the park because two pupils had forgotten their forms. Zeynep put up her hand. “That's not fair, Miss. Why should everyone miss out because of two people?” The teacher's face stayed calm. “I understand it feels unfair, Zeynep. But without forms, I cannot take them safely.” Pablo, beside her, whispered, “She's right.” Zeynep folded her arms, then said, “Can we go tomorrow if everyone brings the form?” The teacher smiled. “Yes, let's plan that.” Zeynep breathed out. She still felt cross, but she understood.

qa.q: Why could the class not go to the park?
qa.a: Two pupils had forgotten their forms.

qa.q: What was Zeynep feeling when she objected, and what did she still feel after the answer?
qa.a: She felt it was unfair for everyone to miss out, and she remained a bit cross even though she understood the safety reason.

qa.q: What did Zeynep do that showed a good way to object?
qa.a: She used respectful words, asked a question and then suggested going tomorrow if everyone brought the form.

qa.q: How might the teacher see Zeynep's objection?
qa.a: The teacher stayed calm and listened, so she probably saw it as a fair concern and a chance to plan another day.

grounding: A child objects to what seems unfair and understands why something is forbidden, using respectful words.

passage: In the school hostel, the warden, Ms. Nikita, told the Class 6 boys that no phones could be used after eight. Gautam had a video call from his grandmother booked every Sunday at nine, and he wanted to keep it. He waited until the others had gone and then said, “Ma'am, I don't want to break your rule. May I ask if my Sunday call with my grandmother could be an exception?” Ms. Nikita thought. “The rule is for sleep. I can't change it for one, but I can let you call at seven instead.” Gautam's shoulders eased. “Thank you, Ma'am. Seven is good.”

qa.q: What time did Gautam's call with his grandmother usually happen?
qa.a: Nine on Sundays.

qa.q: What was Gautam feeling as he waited until the others had gone?
qa.a: He was probably a little nervous and wanted to ask respectfully without embarrassment, and he cared about the call with his grandmother.

qa.q: How did Gautam's way of objecting to the rule work in his favour?
qa.a: He began by saying he did not want to break the rule, asked politely and stayed calm when the answer was not a full yes.

qa.q: Why might Ms. Nikita keep the rule but change the time?
qa.a: The rule is for sleep, so she kept its purpose, while making room for Gautam's call.

grounding: A child objects respectfully to a rule, understands why it is there, and gets a workable answer, even though the answer stays no to the original request.

passage: I'm Vikas. On Monday, Sir told Class 5 we couldn't use the big playground at break any more. Everyone groaned. Siddharth stood up. I thought he'd shout, like he does at cricket. Instead he said, “Sir, that feels unfair. Class 6 still uses it. Can you tell us why?” Sir didn't get angry. “Fair question. They're digging for the new water tank near the swings, and your break is when the trucks come in. Class 6 has break after the trucks leave.” Siddharth thought. “Then can we have the small ground instead?” “Yes. That I can do.” The big playground stayed a no. I don't know what Siddharth felt, but he sat down calm.

qa.q: What was being dug near the swings?
qa.a: They were digging for the new water tank near the swings.

qa.q: What was Siddharth likely feeling when he stood up?
qa.a: Siddharth was likely frustrated and felt the rule was unfair, since Class 6 still used the playground.

qa.q: How did Siddharth object in a way that worked?
qa.a: He said calmly that it felt unfair, asked for the reason, then suggested an alternative, the small ground.

qa.q: How did Sir respond to being questioned?
qa.a: Sir called it a fair question, explained the safety reason about the trucks and agreed to the small ground while keeping the no.

grounding: Shows a child objecting to a rule with respectful words, understanding the safety reason, and an adult supporting the objection though the answer stays no.

passage: Friday: Papa said Charu couldn't watch the horror film with her cousins. “NOT FAIR!” she yelled, and slammed her door. Papa didn't come after her. Saturday: Charu wrote a note and slid it under the study door: Papa, everyone else is watching it. Please explain why not. Sachin, her Papa, read it and came out. “Thank you for writing, not yelling. The last scary film gave you nightmares for a week, and you slept in our bed. That's why.” Charu remembered. “It's still a no?” “It's still a no. But you pick the next film for everyone.” Sunday: Charu picked a comedy. Even the cousins laughed.

qa.q: What gave Charu nightmares for a week?
qa.a: The last scary film gave her nightmares for a week.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling when she yelled “NOT FAIR”?
qa.a: Charu felt angry and left out, since her cousins were all watching the film.

qa.q: How did Charu's objection change from Friday to Saturday?
qa.a: She moved from yelling and slamming the door to writing a respectful note asking for the reason.

qa.q: How did Sachin respond to the note?
qa.a: Sachin thanked her for writing instead of yelling, explained the reason, kept the no and let her choose the next film.

grounding: Shows a child learning to object with respectful words, and a parent supporting that even when the answer stays no.

passage: Keerthana, you were right to tell the coach it wasn't fair. Let your Jaya Paati tell you about my science club. When I was twelve, our headmaster made a rule: only boys could join, because girls might break the glass tubes. I was so angry I wanted to throw a tube myself. Instead, my mother helped me write a letter. I took it to his office and said, “Sir, I respectfully object. I've never broken anything. Please let me try for one month.” He looked at me over his spectacles for a long time. Then he said, “One month.” I didn't break a single tube. By the next year, six girls had joined.

qa.q: How long did the headmaster first let Jaya try?
qa.a: He let her try for one month.

qa.q: What was young Jaya feeling about the boys-only rule?
qa.a: She felt angry at the unfairness, so angry she wanted to throw a tube herself.

qa.q: What choice did young Jaya make, and why did it work?
qa.a: She wrote a letter and objected respectfully in person, asking for a fair trial, which the headmaster granted.

qa.q: What might the headmaster have thought as he looked over his spectacles?
qa.a: He may have been surprised by her calm, respectful objection and decided it deserved a fair chance.

grounding: Shows a child objecting to unfair treatment with respectful words, supported by an adult.

passage:
The monsoon storm had knocked the power out at the school hostel, and the girls wanted to watch the lightning from the roof. Warden Aunty stood at the stairs. "No roof tonight."

Shreya stamped. "That's so unfair!"

Kashish touched her arm, then turned to the warden. "Aunty, may I say something? We saw the Class 8 boys on their roof ten minutes ago. If they can go, why can't we?"

Warden Aunty raised her eyebrows. "Thank you for telling me politely. Nobody should be on any roof in lightning. It can strike the highest point." She called the boys' warden right then. "The answer stays no, for everyone. But you were right to object."

Kashish nodded. Shreya grumbled, but more quietly.

qa.q: Who had Kashish seen on their roof?
qa.a: The Class 8 boys, ten minutes earlier.

qa.q: What was Shreya feeling when she stamped and said, "That's so unfair!"?
qa.a: Frustrated and angry at being stopped, especially as it seemed a rule only for the girls.

qa.q: What made Kashish's objection effective?
qa.a: She asked politely, gave a specific fact about the boys and stayed calm, so the warden listened and fixed the unfairness.

qa.q: How did Warden Aunty see Kashish's objection?
qa.a: As fair and respectful; she thanked her, explained the lightning danger and called the boys' warden, even though the answer stayed no.

grounding: It shows a child objecting to unfair treatment with respectful words, and an adult supporting the objection while explaining why the roof stays forbidden.
